MCP server for SAP Datasphere: access data as the logged-in user with principal propagation

Options
Wednesday
SarahMakarem
Newcomer
985 Views
0 Comments
5 Likes
  • SAP Managed Tags

Labels
  • GenAI Assisted Content

  • Technology Updates​

 

AI clients such as Claude can use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to call tools. A tool that reads business data raises an obvious question: whose permissions does it use? A shared technical user is simple, but then every question to the AI runs with the same, usually too broad, authorization.

In this post we set up everything an MCP server needs to read data from SAP Datasphere as the logged-in user. Datasphere sees the person's own account and applies their own space permissions. The setup builds on the SAP blog Integrating with SAP Datasphere Consumption APIs using SAML Bearer Assertion. We describe the steps in order, and we mark where we had to deviate from that blog and why.

How it works

The MCP server acts on behalf of the user. The user's identity travels along a chain of systems up to Datasphere, so that Datasphere applies the user's own permissions. This concept is called principal propagation.

Every question to the AI client runs through five steps. The MCP server never creates an identity itself, it only passes on who asked.

 

 

  1. Login: The user logs in once, not on every question about Datasphere data. The login runs through the BTP login service (XSUAA), on to SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) and to the corporate identity provider. We used Microsoft Entra ID, but any identity provider that IAS supports works. The identity provider confirms who is logging in via SAML, and IAS adds the user's groups.
  2. Tool call: The user asks the AI client a question about Datasphere data. The client passes it to the MCP server as a tool call.
  3. Login token: During the login in step 1, the BTP login service issued the login token and handed it to the MCP server, which stores it locally. It contains the identity and the groups of the user. When the tool call arrives, the MCP server fetches the stored token and uses it for the next step.
  4. Principal propagation: The MCP server sends the login token to the BTP Destination service. The Destination service builds a signed SAML assertion from it, which is proof "on behalf of this user", and exchanges it at Datasphere for a Datasphere token. Datasphere matches the user by a unique identifier, in our case the email address. The platform handles the cryptographically demanding parts, so the server needs neither key material nor its own SAML code.
  5. Response with authorized data: The server calls the Datasphere Consumption API with the Datasphere token. Datasphere checks the permissions of the user and returns only the data the user may access. The AI client uses it to answer the question.

In detail, each system in the chain only accepts proof from the system it trusts, and issues a new proof for the next one.

 

Phase 1, login (once): The browser opens the XSUAA login page of the BTP subaccount. XSUAA redirects to SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS), and IAS redirects on to the identity provider. The provider confirms the user's identity with a SAML assertion, IAS adds the group sac, and XSUAA issues a BTP token with the user's email and groups. The MCP server stores it locally.

Phase 2, data access (on every tool call): The MCP server sends the BTP token together with its own service token to the BTP Destination service. The Destination service builds a SAML assertion, signs it with the certificate of the subaccount and exchanges it at Datasphere for a Datasphere token. Datasphere finds the user by email and grants permissions only if the group sac is present. With that token the MCP server calls the Consumption API on behalf of the user.

Set up the trust relationships first

The flow only works if each system trusts the one before it. The trust is set up once, and Datasphere knows neither the identity provider nor IAS. It only trusts the BTP subaccount. Set up every trust relationship that does not exist yet, as described in the table. The rest of this post covers the parts that are specific to this scenario.

 

WhotrustsSet up inGuide
IASthe identity providerCorporate identity provider, conditional authenticationEstablish trust between Microsoft Entra ID and IAS
XSUAA (BTP subaccount)IASTrust configuration in the BTP cockpit (OpenID Connect)Establish trust between BTP and IAS
Dataspherethe BTP subaccountTrusted identity provider with the subaccount's signing certificate, OAuth client with purpose API Access and SAML2.0 BearerIntegrating with SAP Datasphere Consumption APIs using SAML Bearer Assertion
 

We tested the whole chain with Microsoft Entra ID as the identity provider. You can use any provider that IAS supports as a corporate identity provider. What matters is that there is trust between the identity provider and IAS.

Two details decide whether this works, so keep them in mind:

  • Datasphere only grants permissions if the SAML assertion contains the group sac.
  • Datasphere finds the user by a unique identifier. We use the email address, which Entra ID delivers and which ends up in the user_name claim of the XSUAA token. It must be identical in the identity provider, in IAS and in Datasphere.

Prerequisites

  • SAP Datasphere tenant and admin rights (System → Administration, Security → Users)
  • BTP subaccount with admin rights (Trust Configuration, Destinations, service instances)
  • An SAP Cloud Identity Services (IAS) tenant. You need admin rights for step 4. If you have none, ask an IAS admin to do that one step.

Replace the placeholders in <...> with your own values:


PlaceholderMeaning
<ias-tenant>Your IAS tenant, for example abc12345.accounts.ondemand.com
<subaccount-subdomain>Subdomain of your BTP subaccount
<dsp-host>Host of your Datasphere tenant, for example mytenant.eu20.hcs.cloud.sap
 

Part 1: Datasphere user and roles

Step 1. Check that your user exists, with the right email

  1. In Datasphere open Security → Users.
  2. Find your user (or create it) and check the Email column.

The email has to be identical to the one in IAS. Otherwise Datasphere cannot match the user from the SAML assertion and returns 401.

 

Step 2. Assign the roles for the Consumption API

  1. Open Security → Users, select your user and choose Roles.
  2. Assign the Consumption API User permission through a role in your space.
  3. Assign Data Warehouse Cloud Consumer (single space) or Scoped Data Warehouse Cloud Consumer (several spaces).

Pitfall: without the Consumption API permission, every data query fails with 403 Forbidden, even for administrators and modelers. Authentication is fine at that point, so it is easy to look in the wrong place.

 

Part 2: Trust between BTP and IAS, and the group sac

Step 3. Check the trust configuration

  1. BTP cockpit → your subaccount → Security → Trust Configuration.
  2. Your IAS tenant must be listed and available for user logon.

If it is missing, choose Establish Trust and select your IAS tenant. SAP describes the wizard in Establish Trust and Federation Between SAP Authorization and Trust Management Service and SAP Cloud .... It uses OpenID Connect, so you do not exchange SAML metadata.

 

Establishing the trust also creates an application in IAS that represents the subaccount. You find it under Applications & Resources → Applications. It uses OpenID Connect: 

 

Step 4. Add the attribute Groups = sac in IAS

Establishing the trust created an application in IAS, named SAP BTP subaccount <subaccount-subdomain>. We add an attribute there.

  1. IAS admin console → Applications & Resources → Applications.
  2. Open the application of the BTP subaccount.
  3. Open Attributes and add the attribute Groups with the value sac. Save.

     

XSUAA copies the IAS groups into its token (xs.system.attributes.xs.saml.groups). The Destination service later passes them on in the SAML assertion.

 

 

Part 3: Trust between the BTP subaccount and Datasphere

Step 5. Export the IDP metadata of the subaccount

  1. BTP cockpit → subaccount → Connectivity → Destination Trust → SAML IDP Trust Configuration.
  2. Choose Export.

The XML file contains the provider name and the signing certificate of the subaccount. The Destination service signs the SAML assertions with this certificate.

 

The exported file contains the provider name and the certificate:

 

Image source: SAP blog Integrating with SAP Datasphere Consumption APIs using SAML Bearer Assertion,

 

Step 6. Add the subaccount as trusted identity provider in Datasphere

  1. Datasphere → System → Administration → App Integration.
  2. Under Trusted Identity Providers choose Add a Trusted Identity Provider.
  3. Enter a name. Copy Provider Name and Signing Certificate from the XML file. Save.

 

The same values entered in Datasphere:

 

Image source: SAP blog Integrating with SAP Datasphere Consumption APIs using SAML Bearer Assertion,

Part 4: The Datasphere OAuth client

Step 7. Create the OAuth client

  1. Datasphere → System → Administration → App Integration → OAuth Clients → Add a New OAuth Client.

  2. Fill in:

    FieldValue
    Namefor example mcp-datasphere
    PurposeAPI Access
    AccessData Export Service
    Authorization GrantSAML2.0 Bearer
     

  3. Save, and copy Client ID and Secret right away. The secret is shown only once.

Note: purpose Interactive Usage does not work for us. It only offers the Authorization Code grant, and the token exchange fails with Unauthorized grant type. According to the original blog, Interactive Usage only works for clients created before release 2024.13.

Image source: SAP blog Integrating with SAP Datasphere Consumption APIs using SAML Bearer Assertion, © SAP SE.

Step 8. Note the two SAML URLs

Above the OAuth client list Datasphere shows two URLs. Copy both:

  • OAuth2SAMLTokenURL, ending in /oauth/token/alias/<...>
  • OAuth2SAMLAudience

Part 5: The BTP destination

Step 9. Create the destination

  1. BTP cockpit → subaccount → Connectivity → Destinations → Create Destination.

  2. Enter:

    PropertyValueNote
    NameDatasphere_Token_Exchange_MCPYour MCP server needs this name later
    TypeHTTP 
    URLhttps://<dsp-host>Deviation: host only. The MCP server appends the API paths itself.
    Proxy TypeInternet 
    AuthenticationOAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion 
    AudienceOAuth2SAMLAudience from step 8Deviation: exactly this one URL. A list of several URLs caused None of the audiences ... matched.
    AuthnContextClassRefurn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:ac:classes:PreviousSession 
    Client KeyClient ID from step 7 
    Token Service URLOAuth2SAMLTokenURL from step 8Deviation: it must be the /alias/... URL. Otherwise: No subject confirmation methods were met.
    Token Service UserClient ID from step 7 
    Token Service PasswordClient secret from step 7If you get Bad credentials, re-enter it. Editing the destination can clear it.
     

  3. Under Additional Properties add:

    PropertyValueNote
    HTML5.DynamicDestinationtrue 
    HTML5.SetXForwardedHeadersfalse 
    userIdSourceuser_nameDeviation: the XSUAA token carries the email address from Microsoft Entra ID in its user_name claim, so the destination reads the user from there. Without it: Cannot determine user to propagate.
    nameIdFormaturn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:1.1:nameid-format:unspecifiedDeviation: the value of user_name is passed on as it is, and Datasphere matches the user by it.
     

    Note: userIdSource and nameIdFormat depend on where your identity provider puts the user identifier in the token. In our setup Microsoft Entra ID delivers the email address, and it ends up in the user_name claim of the XSUAA token. If your provider delivers another identifier, such as the login name, check which claim holds it and adjust both properties. The same identifier must exist in Datasphere.

  4. Save.

How the Datasphere values map to the destination fields:

Part 6: BTP service instances

The MCP server needs two instances. XSUAA lets the user log in. The Destination service lets the server read the destination.

Step 10. Create the XSUAA instance and a service key

  1. BTP cockpit → subaccount → Instances and Subscriptions → Create.

  2. Service Authorization and Trust Management Service, plan application, and a name such as xsuaa-instance-mcp.

  3. Parameters:

    {
  "xsappname": "mcp-datasphere",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated"
}

  4. Open the instance → Service Keys → Create. Note url, clientid and clientsecret.

Deviation: the original blog uses an approuter for the login. An MCP server that logs the user in from a local browser needs a redirect URI in the instance, for example http://localhost:8765/callback. Use the one your server expects.

Image source: SAP blog Integrating with SAP Datasphere Consumption APIs using SAML Bearer Assertion

 

 

Step 11. Create the Destination service instance and a service key

  1. Instances and Subscriptions → Create: service Destination Service, plan lite.
  2. Open the instance → Service Keys → Create. Note url, uri, clientid and clientsecret.

 

 

Image source: SAP blog Integrating with SAP Datasphere Consumption APIs using SAML Bearer Assertion, © SAP SE.

Part 7: Connect your MCP server

This post does not ship an MCP server. Any MCP server can use the setup above, as long as it does two things in this order: first it logs the user in, then it accesses Datasphere on behalf of that user.

Step 12. Make the values available to your MCP server

Your MCP server needs the values from the service keys and the destination. Put them where your server can read them, for example environment variables or a secret store:

ValueSource
XSUAA url, clientid, clientsecretXSUAA service key (step 10)
Destination service url, uri, clientid, clientsecretDestination service key (step 11)
Destination nameDestination from step 9
 

These values contain secrets. Keep them out of version control.

Step 13. Log in first, then access Datasphere

  1. Log the user in through XSUAA. Use the OpenID Connect authorization code flow with the XSUAA values. For a server on the user's machine, add the redirect URI from step 10. Store the token and refresh it when it expires.
  2. Check the token. Decode the access token and check two claims. user_name must be the user's email address, equal to the one in Datasphere. xs.system.attributes.xs.saml.groups must contain sac.
  3. Get a Datasphere token. On every tool call, call the Destination service with two tokens: its own service token (Authorization: Bearer) and the user's token (X-user-token).
  4. Call the Consumption API with the Datasphere token from the response.

Pitfall: if the login fails with a 401, check how your server authenticates at XSUAA. XSUAA client IDs contain characters such as ! and |. With HTTP Basic authentication they get URL-encoded and the login fails. Send the credentials in the request body (client_secret_post) instead.

To see whether Datasphere granted the user's permissions, decode the Datasphere token. If its scope contains more than openid and uaa.user, the permissions were granted.

What happens on every tool call

  1. The MCP server reads your XSUAA token from the cache.
  2. It calls the Destination service with two tokens: its own service token (Authorization: Bearer) and your user token (X-user-token).
  3. The Destination service extracts your email and groups (userIdSource=user_name), builds a SAML assertion with Groups=sac and that identifier (the email address) as NameID, and signs it with the subaccount certificate.
  4. It sends the assertion to the Datasphere token endpoint with the grant type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:saml2-bearer, plus the OAuth client ID and secret.
  5. Datasphere checks the signature against the trusted identity provider (step 6), finds the user by email and issues a token with that user's scopes.
  6. The MCP server calls the Consumption API with that token.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Cannot determine user to propagateNo user ID found in the tokenuserIdSource=user_name (step 9)
None of the audiences ... matchedSeveral audience URLsOnly the OAuth2SAMLAudience (step 8 )
No subject confirmation methods were metToken Service URL without /alias/...Use OAuth2SAMLTokenURL (step 8 )
Bad credentialsWrong or cleared Token Service PasswordRe-enter the client secret (step 9)
Unauthorized grant typeOAuth client purpose is Interactive UsageCreate an API Access client (step 7)
401, token scope only openid / uaa.userNo Groups=sac in the assertionStep 4, and log in through XSUAA
403 on data queriesConsumption API permission missingStep 2
 

Summary

With an OAuth client for the SAML2.0 Bearer grant, a destination of type OAuth2SAMLBearerAssertion and a login through XSUAA, an MCP server can call Datasphere with the identity of the person who asked. No technical user and no shared secret for data access are needed, and the Datasphere authorizations stay in force.

The details that cost us the most time were small ones: the group sac, the email as the user key, the /alias/ token URL, and the purpose API Access of the OAuth client. Check these first when something fails.

I am happy to hear about your experience in the comments, especially if you run this with another identity provider in front of IAS.
